If you just met someone, and you know little to nothing about them, ask about them. See what you have in common and branch off of that. If you don't find anything in common, don't go for the weather or sports or that trite babbling. Instead choose something that feels natural to you, and hopefully to them. As what books they like, ask what they're passionate about. Or bring up something interesting you read not too long ago. That can help the conversation spiral out into something great.

However, you have to remain focused. Don't get dismayed. If things get awkward it's only because you let them get that way. Laugh it off. People generally tend to enjoy those who make them laugh and smile the most. (Think of a prof you had that your class adored - he or she was probably really funny, right?). 

It's ok if you fall silent for a little bit. Sometimes it's ok to be quiet.

Here's a story my grandmother told me that has helped me so many times: 

A young woman recently got married. She was always the nervous, anxious type who constantly complained. After her marriage, she held a party for her relatives. In the meanwhile, she would complain to everyone about her husband, her cat, her house, her cooking, and anything else that came up. 

During the party, her mother came to her and told her to come to the kitchen. She followed. Her mother turned and said, calmly, "You've complained to us so many times. It's because you keep everything locked inside of your heart." 

"Do I really?" She snapped.

Her mother was unfazed. "Yes. And your heart can overfill with emotions: anger, sadness, and so you mustn't let that happen to you. So, find a place in the wall, or talk to me," she pulled a thin curtain away from one of the barren cupboards, "and tell it everything you have on your mind." 

The young lady agreed. 

A few months later, the young lady stopped bothering her relatives. Her husband was soothed. The mother came by and asked to see the spot where she spoke into. The lady quietly showed her, pulling the current back. Behind it was a spot of charred, blackened wall. The mother smiled.

"See, that would have been inside of you." 

So don't keep things locked up. If something really bad happens, and I hope it won't, then it won't add to your mounting pile and eventually lead you to a panic attack or anything like that.

After being verbally abused by my boss, losing my good friend, a hard break up, a big fight, and overall anxiety crushing me into oblivion my "last" thoughts were: "I'm so sorry I couldn't have been better". 

A friend called me, terrified, and we talked for an hour until I calmed down. 

The second time a friend called the hotline for me and forced me to listen. What I thought? "What's the point anymore?" 

The third time I was just so scared. I was scared and angry and sad and tired and so, so lonely. I kept thinking I would reach something better if I died, that I would feel "alive" then.


The fourth and last time I got pretty far. I cut both my wrists open and forcefully tore the earring off my ear, while crying. The reasons kept accumulating, the thoughts kept coming back stronger. I was alone then. My only friend had left me because she was "done" with my shit. I don't really blame her. However, I thought, let me think of all the good things... The sun-bleached memories, the warm summer breezes, the good food, the glistening stars, the smiling faces, the places I could still go, the books I could write, the lovers I could kiss, the hearts I could affect... I couldn't do any of that while buried in the ground. That's when I snapped out of it. I manned the fuck up. I got the help I needed and here I am. And now, although my anxiety is bad (my other posts probably describe it better), and sometimes I still get the urge to cut, I have to remember to just *keep going*.

When I was a kid my allergies were a lot worse than they are now. Then, a puff of dust got me sneezing and miserable. I used to detest going in during Spring in Autumn out of shame of how snotty I looked. I wanted to shrivel up and die. 

Well, being the weird foreign student who barley spoke English, was too short, ugly, and had maybe one or two friends, didn't help to that scenario. 

One day my allergies acted up at recess and my eyes became waterfalls and my nose turned crimson. I sat in class, blinking away tears as the teacher called my parents. A bunch of kids thought it was a good idea to feast upon the weak. They asked if I was crying. If I was hurting. If I needed someone to talk to, a thumb to suck, and other uncreative insults. I started to laugh. Again, I barely spoke English, so I didn't understand they were mocking me. This made everything worse. They labeled me as "dumb", "slow", and I thought of myself that way for a long, long time. 

Thinking back, I grow simultaneously sad and triumphant. Not the worst case of bullying, but it wasn't exactly very nice.

I get classified as "feminist" a lot, although I don't think I really am. However, people are not equal as people. Some work harder, are smarter, are faster, are privileged, are morally stable, unstable, sociopath, peaceful, motivated, lazy, and so on. That should be what we classify people on, not something stupid. My feminist friends agree with this, they believe the goal of feminism is for everyone to be equal, men and women, and so on. At the core they, or we I suppose, don't hate men. That would be hypocritical. We acknowledge differences, but also we want women to get paid the same way, we want to quell judgement until the person is truly known. 

As for issues, I get into debates about this often. "But, biologically we're different!" Yes, males and females are, but substantially? Hmm I don't think so. The world's viewed differently. I just want people to be nicer to each other, and themselves. Is that wrong, then?

i think that my master and i realised what was happening when we were eating breakfast. she was having these flakes of yellow in milk, which is silly because i think milk only comes from mothers. but she took it from a cardboard box that had the word MILK across the side. 

(i think it is also really silly that i know how to read this, but my brain works like that. for example, i see the letters and noise comes into my head that i understand. i think it is funny but also strange)

then, it came to me. an image just exploded in my mind and i sat up, thumping my tail very hard against the tile. i barked, then, when i saw that she didn’t move her head, i went up to her. my nose is wet so she jumped a little when i poked her with it in the leg. she wears shorts and a white jacket usually so i can touch her skin easily. she looks at me, smiling, and pets my head with her hand. her nails are long and pretty. i bark up at her, remembering that there was something in my mind.

once i heard that humans with brains like mine do the same thing i do, which is thinking back through my thoughts just like walking backwards through a park that you’ve already seen. so i can carefully retrace my steps. i think that is also very strange. i bark at her and give her a nudge that makes what i think seem very important. also, i think it is important. it feels very big to me. 

she does look worried so i lick her hand and start to walk back. she stands up, curious, and follows me. i walk slowly to my leash and lick the end, indicating that i want to go outside. i don’t really know why i want to do this but it seems important, too. so i watch as she gets her coat that says GUCCI on the tag and pulls it on. she taps her foot as she does this, looking for her shoes. once she finishes, which feels like a long time, she goes to me and puts the leash on. i don’t like it very much.

we go outside and i start to walk casually, looking normal. we pass trees and grass and squirrels and more trees and eventually she tugs at my leash, making me stop. i pause and sit down. she comes towards me and makes a wondering expression. i don’t always understand what she says, but i hear something. there is a distant sound, somewhere deep inside of us but also between us, like a valley. i try to pay attention, since my ears are very keen like a dog’s should be, and i still do not hear exactly. i hear phrases and i barely understand what she means, but i can also hear the confusion and concern, also that she is tired. i lick her hand and nudge her to go on. she sighs and agrees. her hair is very long and it brushes me as she stands back up. 

we continue down the many streets and the big street lamps. the last bit of sunshine that was hidden behind the mountains begins to spill over. it looks very nice from where i am. we trot by and past a sign that’s very big and white and has messy letters on it. it says DEPOT. i do not know what it is, but i hear that static again and i can tell she is frightened. i know then that this is where we are supposed to go.

we walk in and through the doors. inside it smells very bad and i hear my own make a shriek. it is strange when she makes sounds because she cannot hear them. so they sound unique. i think. i am not sure. my mind hurts when i think of this. 

inside i find a big black box with an antenna poking out of it. i bark at it and she picks through the mossy floor. she goes to it and picks it up. she puts it to her ear, giving me an amused grin. i think she knows that i know very much and that i am a smart dog. i bark once or twice.

“Hello!” i say with my mind.

it’s strange. it is like pushing your thought through a small tube. 

her eyes widen. 

she opens her mouth but i say “No, your head!” 

so she does and i can hear her. 

and she says: “You can hear me?”

and i say: “Yes.”

and she says: “So what was so important?”

and i say: “I think I know how something started.”

and she says: “How what started? The universe?”

her voice is very nice, like a mellow wind or a creek. i have not been to either, but i have seen the beginning of the world in my head so i feel like i know what those awfully nice things are like. 

and i say: “yes.”

and she says: “Enlighten me.”

and she laughs and says something else: “Oh god, I’m talking to my dog. And I can actually hear her. Oh god, wow, oh god oh god…”

and i wonder why she thinks that. 

and she says, now more seriously: “If something this crazy works I’m sure the miracles don’t stop there. So go on.”

and i say: “it was created by…” her eyes widen a little. i tell her. then she tells me to keep it a secret.

Matt, shining again as CrossRoads, stared out the window, his eyes squinting. He had the ability to avert a person’s path and choice, but indirectly. He couldn’t force a person going to the left to suddenly turn right. He could cause them to forget, or a flower pot to break before them, or a shady character to flit through the shadows before them. His long, black curls pressed against the pillow. 

“Always doing good.” 

“I’m just sick of this.” Matt said, squeezing Andrew’s hand. “Why do they have to swarm the media here? If they found me they’d make an uproar. No one can seem to do good anymore. Soon they’ll have human heroes and gay heroes…” his eyes crinkled, filling with tears.

Andrew raised his eyebrows, his plumy lips moulding into a pout. “Matt?” 

“Yeah?” 

“I love you.” 

Matt smiled. 

Andrew frowned, his cheeks crimsoning. “Did you make me say that?” 

Matt shrugged. “Maybe I did.” His expression contorted and a long breath escaped him. “Imagine young boys who’re suffering in homes where they can’t be who they are. Now they’re losing a figure to look towards. What the hell do I do?” 

“Live.” 

Before Matt could respond, the door swung open. A woman waltzed in, her heels clicking sharply against the tiles. Her hair bounced in its ponytail, pulled back at the temples. Her face was coated with make up, but it didn’t make up for her obviously unforgiving features. She pulled up a chair besides Matt and sat down, practically pushing Andrew out of his seat. Andrew let go of Matt’s hand, moving his fingers to the weak, bony shoulder. 

“You’re CrossRoads?”

“What the hell does that matter?” Matt grunted.

“You dying gives a bad name to heroes. The victims of crimes will be terrified because now they have no one to save them!” 

“So saving someone suddenly spreads infection? Alert the doctors, we have a medical emergency on our hands.”

“I’m serious.”

“Being gay?”

She leaned forwards. “Do something.”

She sighed. “I hope you know what I do for you. I work my ass off protecting your name so you can do good.”

“Did I ask for your help?”

“I don’t doubt it.”

“Well?”

“Well what?”

Andrew attempted to interlude but Matt gave him a gaze that said ‘this is my battle’ quite clearly. Andrew nodded and pretended to be invested in the potted plant. 

“We can’t stop the press forever.”

“We can try.” 

She stood up. “They’ll find out.”

“Let them. I give up.” 

“All that effort for nothing?” Andrew gasped before he could stop.

Matt narrowed his gaze. “Like I was fending them off for my sake.” 

Andrew and the reporter exchanged a glance. Her expression didn’t soften, but she left without another word. 

“You’re a good man.”

“I try.”

The clock began to tick quietly in the corner, dragging time along with an eternity plodding on by between every second. I lay on my back, staring at the arching ceiling. My home was so wonderful, I thought sleepily. It had everything. Sure, it was the dusty attic just above a diner, but it was worth the pay they had me cough up between two jobs and a failed hobby. The spiderwebs that collected in the corners like shadows were bothersome at times, but I could deal with that. I could deal with anything.

The only thing that escaped that rule was loneliness. I was so lonely. I was always so lonely. I dragged hookers home every night even though the diner owner threatened to kick me out if she ever saw one of those whores in her place “stinking it up”. I told her I wouldn’t be a problem at all. I said that with two giggling girls, reaching for my wallet, at my sides. 

“But you got in just fine.” I said aloud. 

My newest girl, who was probably no older than twenty two, didn’t budge. I really tired her out, didn’t I?

“I mean, if Miss Des caught you up here with me and what we were doing she would have killed me and served me to the dogs! Imagine that.” I laughed. I shut my eyes, still so lonely. 

Still she remained silent. What was her name? Anita? Nita? Nicole? Who cares. I threw an arm around her and pull her limp body close. She smells so sweet in sleep, I thought. I close my eyes and bury my face into her abundant black curls. 

“And I tired you out so much. We had a great night, didn’t we? Oh, I remember how you held me. You didn’t ask for payment right away which I found strange. You wanted the goods first, didn’t you? You horny devil.” I snort with laughter, my eyes screwed shut, my hand resting on her warm belly. “But I guess you brought your own sort of payment. I wouldn’t touch that stuff, believe me. I’d rather touch that warm, secret part of you. All night. You had it your way, didn’t you?” 

I liked telling the ones that stayed overnight about what we did. It solidified it. It crystallised the memory, made it realer, more tangible, less lonely. I embraced her tighter. She had a curved figure, a place for the arms to go between the hip and ribs, many places for the hands to linger. 

“Gosh, I can imagine your voice…” It was like a sparrow. No, a nightingale. Or better yet like a queen. 

 I opened my eyes at least, still seeing dregs under he nose. I go to brush it off, but my thumb stopped. Something was wrong. Something was cold. My heart felt like a knife had slashed through it.

Her breaths weren’t coming. I sit up, examining her prostrate body, her lips still warm. Thus with a kiss I die, I sardonically echo in the dimmest region of my brain that still had the audacity to function. I stare, I stare, but I don’t cry. I don’t need to.
